blocks.content: docker inspect returns the full metadata Docker knows about an image, as structured JSON, everything from its environment variables to its default command to its exact layer list.
Where docker history tells you how an image was built layer by layer, docker inspect tells you what the image actually is right now: a full JSON document describing its configuration.

blocks.alt: One command, the complete metadata behind an image

blocks.content:
docker inspect myapp:1.0
# Returns a JSON array with fields like Config, RootFS,
# Architecture, Created, and Size.

code.content:
docker inspect myapp:1.0
# Returns a JSON array with fields like Config, RootFS,
# Architecture, Created, and Size.

codes.bash:
docker inspect myapp:1.0
# Returns a JSON array with fields like Config, RootFS,
# Architecture, Created, and Size.

blocks.content: The most useful sections are usually Config (environment variables, the default Cmd and Entrypoint, exposed ports), RootFS (the list of layer hashes making up the image), and Architecture (which CPU architecture the image was built for, relevant on mixed x86/ARM infrastructure).

blocks.alt: Config, RootFS, and Architecture are the fields you reach for most

blocks.content: 3. When You Actually Reach for This
blocks.text: 3. When You Actually Reach for This

blocks.content: The most common real use is answering "what exactly is going to run when this container starts": what ENV variables got baked in, what the actual CMD or ENTRYPOINT is, without having to dig back through the original Dockerfile (which you may not even have access to, if you only have the built image).

blocks.alt: Answering exactly what will run, without the original Dockerfile

blocks.content:
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.Env}}' myapp:1.0
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.Cmd}}' myapp:1.0
# --format lets you pull out one specific field instead of
# reading the whole JSON blob.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker inspect exposes the complete configuration of an image as JSON, environment variables, entrypoint, layers, and architecture included.
It is the tool to reach for when you need to know exactly what an image will do at runtime without having its original Dockerfile in front of you.
